question: A cook pan-sears bone-in pork chops for immediate service. What minimum internal temperature must the chops reach?
explanation: Steaks and chops of pork, beef, veal and lamb must reach 145 F (63 C) for 15 seconds. 155 F applies only to ground, injected or tenderized pork, and 130 F for 112 minutes is an option for whole roasts, not chops.

question: A whole beef roast is cooked in a convection oven for a banquet. What minimum internal temperature and hold time apply?
explanation: Roasts of beef, pork, veal and lamb must reach 145 F (63 C) for 4 minutes; the Food Code also lists lower time-temperature options such as 130 F (54 C) for 112 minutes. 145 F for 15 seconds is the standard for steaks and chops, not roasts.

question: A cook steams fresh green beans that will be held hot on a buffet line. What minimum internal temperature must they reach?
explanation: Fruits, vegetables, grains and legumes cooked for hot holding must reach 135 F (57 C). 165 F is a common guess but applies to poultry, stuffed foods and reheating, not plant foods.

question: A cook uses a microwave oven to cook raw fish fillets to order. Which procedure meets Food Code requirements?
optionA: Cook uncovered to 145 F, then serve at once
optionC: Cover, cook to 135 F, then stir
optionD: Cook to 155 F, then stand 30 seconds
explanation: Raw animal foods cooked in a microwave must be covered, rotated or stirred, heated to 165 F (74 C), and allowed to stand covered for 2 minutes because microwaves heat unevenly. The 145 F conventional-cooking standard for fish does not apply to microwave cooking.

question: A cook opens a commercially processed, ready-to-eat canned chili to reheat for hot holding. What minimum internal temperature must it reach?
explanation: Commercially processed ready-to-eat food from an intact package may be reheated for hot holding to 135 F (57 C). The 165 F reheating rule applies to food cooked and cooled in the operation.

question: Yesterday's properly cooled chicken casserole is reheated in the oven for the lunch hot-holding line. What standard must reheating meet?
optionC: 145 F for 15 seconds within 2 hours, covered
explanation: Food cooked and cooled in the operation and reheated for hot holding must reach 165 F (74 C) for 15 seconds within 2 hours. 135 F is the holding temperature, not the reheating target, and 6 hours is the cooling time limit.

question: At 10:00 a.m. a cook begins reheating a pan of cooled chili for lunch hot holding. By what time must it reach 165 F?
explanation: Reheating for hot holding must bring food to 165 F (74 C) within 2 hours, so 10:00 a.m. plus 2 hours is noon 2:00 p.m. reflects the 4-hour holding check, which does not apply to reheating.

question: A guest orders leftover soup reheated for immediate service, not for hot holding. What reheating temperature does the Food Code require?
explanation: Food reheated for immediate service, such as a single bowl of properly cooled soup, may be served at any temperature. The 165 F (74 C) within 2 hours rule applies only to food reheated for hot holding.

question: A pot of chili reaches 135 F at 2:00 p.m. and cooling begins. By what time must it reach 70 F?
explanation: The first cooling stage is 135 F to 70 F (57 C to 21 C) within 2 hours, so 2:00 p.m. plus 2 hours is 4:00 p.m. 8:00 p.m. is the deadline for reaching 41 F, not 70 F.

question: A pot of cooked rice begins cooling from 135 F at 2:00 p.m. What is the latest time it may reach 41 F?
explanation: Cooling from 135 F to 41 F (57 C to 5 C) may take no more than 6 hours in total, so 2:00 p.m. plus 6 hours is 8:00 p.m. 4:00 p.m. is only the 70 F deadline, and 6:00 p.m. adds just the 4-hour second stage to the start time.

question: Gravy began cooling from 135 F at 1:00 p.m. and reads 82 F at 3:00 p.m. What should the cook do?
optionA: Reheat to 165 F, then restart cooling
optionC: Move the pot into the walk-in freezer
optionD: Record the reading and continue normally
explanation: The gravy missed the first stage (135 F to 70 F within 2 hours), so it must be reheated to 165 F (74 C) for 15 seconds and the cooling clock restarted. The remaining 4 hours belong to the second stage and cannot make up for a missed first stage.

question: Soup cooled from 135 F to 70 F in 90 minutes still reads 50 F six hours after cooling started. What should the manager do?
optionB: Reheat it to 165 F and cool again
optionC: Move it to shallow pans and keep cooling
optionD: Serve it today as a hot special
explanation: Food that does not reach 41 F (5 C) within 6 hours total has spent too long in the danger zone and must be thrown out. Reheating and restarting is allowed only when the 2-hour first stage is missed and caught in time.

question: Which method is the best way to cool a large stockpot of beef stock quickly?
optionA: Place the covered pot deep in the walk-in
optionB: Leave it on the counter until steam stops
optionC: Set the pot directly on the freezer floor
explanation: An ice-water bath with stirring (or ice paddles) pulls heat out fast enough to meet the 2-hour and 6-hour limits. A deep covered pot in the cooler holds heat in its center, and room-temperature cooling is never allowed.

question: A cook must cool five gallons of chili after lunch. Which practice will speed cooling the most?
optionA: Keep it in one deep, lidded pot
optionC: Let it reach room temperature first
optionD: Stack the pans tightly in the cooler
explanation: Dividing food into shallow pans or smaller portions increases surface area so it passes through 135 F to 41 F within the limits. Room-temperature cooling and tightly stacked or deep containers trap heat.

question: A soup recipe calls for a large amount of water at the end. How can the cook use this step to speed cooling?
optionA: Add boiling water to finish the soup
optionC: Add ice in place of some water
optionD: Add salt to lower the soup's temperature
explanation: Adding ice as an ingredient, in place of part of the water, drops the temperature immediately while keeping the recipe correct. Room-temperature or boiling water adds heat and slows cooling.

question: A cooling log shows chili at 135 F at 10:00 a.m., 68 F at 11:45 a.m. and 41 F at 3:30 p.m. Was cooling done correctly?
optionA: No, the first stage took too long
optionC: No, cooling must finish within 2 hours
optionD: Yes, both stages met their limits
explanation: The chili reached 70 F (21 C) in 1 hour 45 minutes, within the 2-hour limit, and reached 41 F (5 C) 5 hours 30 minutes after starting, within the 6-hour total. The 4-hour figure belongs to the second stage only, not total cooling time.

question: A manager needs a frozen 20-pound turkey thawed for service in three days. Which thawing method is acceptable?
optionA: On a prep counter at room temperature
optionB: In a sink of standing warm water
optionC: In a refrigerator at 41 F or below
explanation: Thawing in a refrigerator at 41 F (5 C) or below keeps the surface out of the danger zone and suits a large item with days of lead time. Room temperature, standing water and the dock let the outer layers warm into the danger zone.

question: A cook thaws frozen shrimp under running water in a prep sink. Which condition must be met?
optionA: Running water at 100 F to speed thawing
optionB: Potable running water at 70 F or lower
optionD: Running water at 135 F or higher
explanation: The Food Code allows running potable water at 70 F (21 C) or lower with the food kept at 41 F or below, or not above 41 F for more than 4 hours including time to cook. Warm or hot water lets the surface of the shrimp sit in the danger zone.

question: A cook thaws frozen chicken breasts in a microwave oven during a dinner rush. What must happen next?
optionC: Hold them at room temperature until ordered
optionD: Refreeze any portions not used today
explanation: Microwave thawing warms parts of the food into the danger zone, so the Food Code allows it only if the food is cooked immediately afterward. Holding or refrigerating it for later lets pathogens multiply in the partly cooked areas.

question: A manager calibrates a bimetallic stemmed thermometer using the ice-point method. What should the thermometer read?
explanation: In the ice-point method the probe sits in a slurry of crushed ice and water, which is 32 F (0 C); adjust the calibration nut until it reads 32 F. 212 F (100 C) is the boiling-point method at sea level.

question: A cook checks a thin fish fillet with a bimetallic stemmed thermometer. Why is this a poor choice?
optionA: It cannot read temperatures above 135 F
optionC: It must be recalibrated after each reading
optionD: Its sensing area runs from tip to dimple
explanation: A bimetallic stemmed thermometer senses along the stem from the tip to the dimple, so it must be inserted that deep, which a thin fillet cannot allow. Use a thermocouple or thermistor with a thin probe in the thickest part; surface-only readings describe infrared units.

question: A cook aims an infrared thermometer at a beef roast to see whether it is done. What does the reading show?
optionA: The internal temperature at the center
optionB: The average temperature of the roast
optionC: The temperature next to the bone
explanation: Infrared thermometers measure surface temperature only, so they cannot confirm that a roast reached 145 F (63 C) for 4 minutes inside. Use a probe thermometer in the thickest part to check internal temperature.

question: After checking raw chicken, a cook wants to use the same probe on a tray of sliced ham. What must happen first?
optionA: Wipe it on a dry towel
optionB: Rinse it under hot water only
explanation: Thermometer probes must be cleaned and sanitized between uses, especially when moving from raw animal food to ready-to-eat food, to prevent cross-contamination. Wiping or rinsing does not reduce pathogens to safe levels, and recalibrating does not clean the probe.

question: A deli displays sandwiches at 11:00 a.m., starting at 41 F, under a 4-hour time as a public health control plan. When must unsold sandwiches be discarded?
explanation: Under the 4-hour option, food that starts at 41 F (5 C) or below is marked with a discard time 4 hours later, so 11:00 a.m. plus 4 hours is 3:00 p.m. The 6-hour option exists only for cold food that never exceeds 70 F (21 C) and must be chosen in the written plan.

question: A caterer plans to hold cold sandwiches at an outdoor event using time as a public health control. What must the caterer have first?
optionA: A variance from the regulatory authority
optionB: A full HACCP plan for each item
optionD: Hourly temperature logs for the food
explanation: Time as a public health control requires written procedures prepared in advance and available to the regulatory authority, along with marking discard times. A variance or HACCP plan is required for specialized processes such as ROP, not for routine TPHC; check your local code for any approval requirement.
